title: Set up a comfortable table
steps: Choose a chair and surface where you can see and reach the cards without leaning or straining.
Try large-print cards, a card holder or a second dealer whenever helpful.
Give a no-timer practice turn. Adjust the layout whenever a player asks.
check: Can everyone see their cards, reach the piles and explain whose turn it is?

title: Suits, ranks, pips and handling
steps: Sort a 52-card deck into four suits. Count 13 ranks per suit.
Separate number cards and faces. Explain that different games assign different values to aces and faces.
Fan, deal, draw, and discard. Compare matching rank with matching suit. Try a six-pair grid.
check: Can you show a pair of equal ranks and two different ranks that share a suit?

title: Counting from ace to ten
steps: Build a face-up line from ace through ten.
Turn some slots face down. Ask which rank belongs in each missing slot.
Switch to a full practice layout and explain where each draw belongs.
check: If the 6 slot holds a face-down card, where does a newly drawn 6 go?

title: Add, subtract and reverse-check
steps: Count each pair aloud and compare results.
Subtract smaller from larger, then use addition to check the difference.
Deal 7 and 5 against 9 and 4. Decide which pair wins under the addition rule and which wins under subtraction.
check: The second pair wins both sample comparisons. Can you change one card to make a different pair win each comparison?

title: Build target totals
steps: Start with a single face-up card and name its complement to ten.
Find two or three cards that reach the target in the grid.
Switch to 15 and explain two different decompositions.
check: For a 7, find a single card and two different cards that each complete a total of 10.

title: Granddad’s running tally
steps: Keep one tally for deadwood and another for the public score across hands.
Recompute the deadwood after every draw and discard in a demonstration hand.
Say which cards were seen, which ones are still unknown, and how that affects a decision to knock.
check: Your deadwood is 8, 7 and ace. You replace 8 with 2. What is the new deadwood total, and what decision does it open?

title: Count suits and remember discards
steps: Use a single deck. Choose a suit and mark the cards of that suit in your hand.
Keep a tally of that suit as each public card is revealed. Include your own known cards once.
Distinguish a card you know was played from a guess about who holds an unknown card.
check: You have four spades, and five other spades have been played. How many spades remain unknown to you?

title: Odds change with the cards you see
steps: Start with a shuffled 52-card deck. The chance of an ace on the first draw is 4/52.
Reveal one ace and one non-ace, then update the count to three aces in fifty unseen cards.
For a one-card draw with no replacement, divide the number of qualifying unseen cards by the total number unseen. Describe how a reshuffle changes the assumptions.
check: Two aces and eight non-aces are visible. The unseen ace probability is 2/42. Explain both numbers.

title: Hi-Lo, running count and true count
steps: Learn the values: 2–6 are +1, 7–9 are 0, and 10–ace are −1.
Start at zero and add the appropriate value when a card is revealed. Check your count in batches.
Divide the running count by the estimated decks remaining. Keep the fraction until the calculation is understood. The practice drill uses no stakes.
check: A running count of +6 with 2.5 decks left gives a true count of +2.4. What changes when the deck is reshuffled?

title: Recover a game from historical evidence
steps: Collect alternate titles, location, date, deck type, and the earliest source you can verify.
Record setup, legal moves, end conditions and scoring as separate claims. Mark every missing step.
If building a playable reconstruction, write down each design choice and cite the evidence next to it.
check: Which statements can you source, and which choices would you make to complete a reconstruction?
